- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.75) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.3) and forecast is overly conservative, slightly increase the early-period mean to avoid premature mean reversion.  
- After a strong upward move in history, forecast should show a slight downward correction in the next 3–5 days, even if sentiment remains bullish.  
- If forecast consistently overshoots true values by >5% in the first 5–7 days, apply a 3–5% downward bias to subsequent days.  
- When sentiment is mixed (0.3–0.75) and history shows volatility, model should average recent 3–5 day trends rather than extrapolating linearly.  
- If true outcome shows a sharp drop after a forecast peak, reduce forecast’s lagged peak by 10–15% to reflect sentiment decay.  
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is neutral or bearish, apply a 2–3% downward bias to avoid overestimating recovery.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated bullish spikes followed by bearish corrections, model should anticipate a 2–4 day lagged reversal in price.
